### From an environmental standpoint, conventional plastics exhibit extremely slow degradation rates in soil and marine environments, often requiring decades or even centuries to decompose. This persistence leads to long-term environmental pollution and accumulation in ecosystems [12].

### 2.2.5 Thermosetting Polymers

Thermosetting polymers undergo irreversible chemical cross-linking during the curing process, forming rigid three-dimensional molecular networks. Once cured, thermosets do not melt upon reheating but instead undergo thermal decomposition. Although thermosetting polymers generally exhibit superior thermal stability compared to thermoplastics, their brittleness and lack of recyclability limit their practical applications [13].

### 2.2.6 Elastomers

Elastomers are polymers characterized by high elasticity and flexibility, such as natural rubber and synthetic elastomers. While these materials can effectively absorb mechanical energy, they are typically combustible and may produce hazardous smoke and gases when exposed to fire conditions [14].

### 2.3 Fire Behavior of Polymers

The fire behavior of polymers is governed by their chemical composition, molecular structure, and thermal properties. When exposed to an external heat source, polymers do not ignite immediately; instead, they undergo a sequence of thermally induced processes.

Initially, the polymer absorbs heat, resulting in a rise in temperature and subsequent softening or melting. Continued heating leads to pyrolysis, during which polymer chains decompose and release flammable gaseous products. These gases mix with ambient oxygen and ignite once favorable temperature and oxygen concentration conditions are achieved [15].
